chapter.title: Lifecycle
chapter.sub: Thirty-one projector failures, a plan due Friday — and eleven years of knowledge about to walk out the door.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  Owner board · Nadia, Maya and Wes · Level L4 · Intermediate support  Thirty-one projector failures this term, a provost who wants a plan by Friday — and Nadia, who has run AV for eleven years, leaving in June with most of what she knows still in her head.  ⚑ RV-135: figures illustrative. RV-124: burnout shown with care.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.stakes: The provost wants a plan by Friday. Nadia leaves in June, and eleven years of knowing how things really work are leaving with her unless someone asks — kindly.
items.reward: A plan built on rates and impact. Nadia's knowledge written down. Nadia still Nadia.

objectives.text: Choose what the plan is built on
Get what Nadia knows — without burning her
Look closer: two things about Nadia's desk

items.rumor: The spreadsheet has the failures. It doesn't have the reason.

items.alt: The AV office early morning: Nadia at her desk holding a printed spreadsheet — 140 projectors, 31 failures.

bubbles.text: The provost wants a plan by Friday. And I told HR this morning — June's my last month.

lines.text: Eleven years. I'm not angry at anyone. I'm just tired, and I'd like to leave before I'm angry.
Then let's make June a good month, not a long one.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #50 · AVERY'S LENS  An average can hide the answer  Before you plan from an average, split it by the things that could matter: model, room, age, use.  31 failures across 140 projectors looked like a replacement program. Split by model, it was 40 projectors and a warranty.

items.prompt: 9:00. What do you build the replacement plan on?
items.risk: A plan that spends the budget on the wrong projectors.
timeout: The spreadsheet sits sorted by date.

options.label: Age: replace the oldest projectors first
options.result: The oldest 30 include only 6 of the ones that actually fail.
options.consequence: Age is a guess about risk.

options.label: Failure rates by model and building, weighed by how many people each failure delays
options.result: Fleet: 0.11. Then you split it — and one model jumps off the page.
options.consequence: Rates tell you where; impact tells you what it costs.

options.label: Ask for money to replace all 140
options.result: The provost's office: “Please come back with a plan that fits the budget.”

items.alt: A bar chart of failures per projector per year: one gray bar for all 140 projectors at 0.11.
items.caption: λ = 31 ÷ (140 × 2) ≈ 0.11. About 15 failures next year — if the fleet were all the same.

items.title: Forty-one sticky notes
items.body: Nadia's monitor frame holds forty-one sticky notes: phone extensions, contract numbers, *X-series — ask R. about boards?*, *don't renew the old signage deal*. Wes photographs every one, with her permission, and types them into the team wiki that afternoon.

items.title: The average hid the answer.
items.body: Split by model, 22 of the 31 failures come from the 40 X-series projectors in the old science building: λ ≈ 0.275. The other 100 run at 0.045. It isn't a fleet problem. It's one model — and in the big halls, each failure delays 240 people.
items.label: Test: what does the split change?

items.alt: The same chart split into three bars: all 140 at 0.11; X-series (40) at 0.275 in red; the other 100 at 0.045 in green.
items.caption: Same tickets. One model.

items.prompt: Honestly? I'd rather just write the whole plan myself. It's my last big thing.

options.label: “It's ours. You tell us what you know in short sessions; Wes and I do the arithmetic. You go home at five.”
options.reply: …Twenty minutes a day. And I'm holding you to five.

options.label: “What's the part only you know?”
options.reply: Vendors. Contracts. Who to call when the portal says no. None of it's written down.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Nadia and Maya beside a board. Failure rate: failures over units times years. Then expected failures next year is lambda times units. Thirty-one failures, a hundred and forty projectors, two years… about point one one each. Fifteen next year. Fifteen classes that stop. Put a cost on each and the provost will listen.

bubbles.text: Failure rate: failures over units times years. Then expected failures next year is lambda times units.
Thirty-one failures, a hundred and forty projectors, two years… about point one one each. Fifteen next year.
Fifteen classes that stop. Put a cost on each and the provost will listen.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Lifecycle plan   Failure rate   End of life   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Failure rate  λ = failures ÷ (units × years) · expected = λ × units × years   λ  failures per unit per year  units  how many devices  years  how long you watched     ƒ FORMULA · Cost of one incident  cost = t fixer  + people × t delay    t fixer   minutes the fixer spends  people  how many people wait  t delay   minutes each waits

items.label: **Learn it now:** failure rates and lifecycle plans.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · tap a plate to open it full size     What the room is telling you     The OSI model applied to video and wireless     Point it at people, not at the ceiling

items.prompt: Wednesday. Nadia knows the vendors, the contracts and the history. She's tired. How do you get what she knows?
items.risk: Losing eleven years in one afternoon in June.

hints.text: How do you move knowledge without spending the person?

options.label: Let her write the plan herself — it's her last big thing
options.result: She stays until ten three nights running. Thursday she calls in sick.
options.consequence: Her knowledge, extracted by burning her.
options.fail: Never spend a person to save a spreadsheet.

options.label: Three twenty-minute sessions; Wes takes notes into the team wiki; she leaves at five
options.result: Twenty minutes into session one: “Oh — the X-series warranty. Did I never forward that?”
options.consequence: Knowledge moves; the person is protected.

options.label: Ask HR to delay her departure
options.result: Nadia hears about it from HR.
options.consequence: Her decision to leave isn't yours to renegotiate.

options.label: Export her mailbox after she's gone
options.result: Eleven years of email, no context, and a privacy officer asking why.
options.consequence: Data without the person's meaning — and without her consent.

items.title: Why things fail when they do
items.body: In 1957 a United States advisory group on the reliability of electronic equipment reported that much military electronics failed early and often — and set out to measure failure rates properly. Reliability engineers came to describe many products with a ‘bathtub curve’: failures high when new, low in mid-life, rising again with wear. A good lifecycle plan asks where on the curve each group of devices sits.

items.alt: Session one, Wednesday afternoon: Nadia talking with open hands; Wes taking notes on a clipboard; Maya listening.

bubbles.text: The X-series have an extended warranty on the lamp-driver boards. Ends the thirtieth of June. I never forwarded it, did I?
Free boards for all forty? If we claim before June?

lines.text: It's free? The boards are just… free, if we ask before June?
If somebody remembers to ask. That was always the whole job.

items.title: It was in Nadia's inbox.
items.body: The fix for the cluster — free lamp-driver boards for all 40 X-series, if claimed before 30 June — existed only in one email thread in Nadia's inbox. The biggest single point of failure in the plan wasn't a projector. It was a tired person nobody had asked.
items.label: Test: what kind of risk is that — and how do you handle it?

items.prompt: Friday, 4 p.m. How do you present next year's failures to the provost?
items.risk: A plan the provost trusts once — or every year.
timeout: You send the spreadsheet without a summary.
The provost reads the total and nothing else.

hints.text: What does an honest estimate include?

options.label: “Zero failures next year.”
options.result: It reads well. It'll be wrong by October — and so will your next plan's credibility.
options.fail: An estimate is not a promise.

options.label: An estimate with its assumptions: about 5 expected (from 15), mostly in seminar rooms; the warranty claim, the halls, spares and monitoring; what could make it wrong
options.result: Provost: “The first plan I've received that tells me what it doesn't know. Approved.”
options.consequence: Honest numbers build trust you'll need next time.

options.label: Just the total cost
options.result: “And what do I get for it?”

options.label: Let Nadia present it alone
options.result: Nadia, on her second-to-last Friday, defending a plan she didn't finish.
options.consequence: Her knowledge, your plan — present it together.

items.alt: The one-page plan: X-series boards under warranty, twelve large-hall projectors, a six-projector spares pool, monitoring — expected failures about five instead of fifteen, with assumptions listed.
items.caption: $48k of $60k. The rest is held for what the estimate got wrong.

items.title: Sent 5:41 p.m.
items.body: *Thank you — this is the first plan I've received that tells me what it doesn't know. Approved. Please thank Nadia for eleven years.* Maya forwards it to Nadia at 5:42. Nadia is already home.

items.alt: Five o'clock Friday. Nadia with her coat on by the door; Maya at her desk.

bubbles.text: It's five. I'm going home. That's the most useful thing I've learned in eleven years.
Go. We've got it written down.

items.alt: The empty arena, three weeks before commencement: a stage being built, banners half hung. Nadia and Wes on the floor.

bubbles.text: Commencement. Two thousand in here, nine thousand on the stream, captions and a second-language channel. My last event. I'd like you to run the stream, Wes.

items.caption: Next: *Commencement.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  λ = failures ÷ (units × years); expected = λ × units × years. Split the average before you plan, weigh failures by the people they delay, present estimates with their assumptions — and move knowledge out of tired people’s heads without spending the people.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Nadia was the single point of failure nobody saw. Who holds knowledge on your team that isn’t written down — and how could you ask for it kindly?
